# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
America wins the AI race on innovation and compute buildout. A patchwork of 50 state regimes raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents. ACIA supports one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT. Ask that it be made permanent (or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before sunset).
- Incident reporting: OPPOSE AS DRAFTED. Ask for a narrow definition of "critical safety incident", a 15-day window (match SB 53, not RAISE's 72 hours), confidentiality and FOIA exemption, and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
- CAISI: SUPPORT voluntary standards role; OPPOSE any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. No position on the dollar figure.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "patchwork", "one national standard", "compliance costs fall hardest on startups", "light-touch, risk-based", "speculative risks".
- Catastrophic-risk scenarios: speculative, and not a sound basis for legislation. Keep the focus on costs and competitiveness.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

 US Federal: Unpacking the Great American AI Act

 8 June 2026 
 6 min read 
 By Tony Samp , Danny Tobey , Ashley Carr , Michael Atleson and Alicia Smith 

 LinkedIn 

 Facebook 

 Twitter 

 Saved to bookmarks . 

 Related topics

 At a glance

 Bipartisan lawmakers have released a 269-page discussion draft of the ‘Great American AI Act’, aiming to establish a comprehensive federal AI framework.

 The draft focuses on national uniformity, workforce impacts, and US leadership, including proposed federal pre-emption of certain state AI laws.

 It introduces transparency and oversight requirements for frontier AI developers, including reporting obligations and mandatory third-party audits.

 The bill includes whistleblower protections and potential civil penalties for non-compliance with key obligations.

 Stakeholder feedback is being sought before formal introduction, although early opposition has already emerged from some groups.

 On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence ( AI ) legislation titled the 'Great American AI Act' ( GAAIA ). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in  supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the  House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition  hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills

 All three sections borrow heavily from  recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable pre-emption provisions

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.

119th CONGRESS
 2d Session
 H. R. 9925

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of

_______________________________________________________________________

 IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

 July 23, 2026

Mr. Obernolte (for himself, Mrs. Trahan, Mrs. Houchin, Mr. Peters, Mr. 
 Scott Franklin of Florida, and Mr. Subramanyam) introduced the 
 following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and 
 Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Science, Space, and 
Technology, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, 
 in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the 
 jurisdiction of the committee concerned

_______________________________________________________________________

 A BILL

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of 
 frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, 
 and for other purposes.

 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the 
United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

 This Act may be cited as the ``Frontier Risk Oversight, National 
Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act'' or the 
``FRONTIER Act''.

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

 In this Act:
 (1) Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.--The 
 term ``acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation'' 
 means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated 
 benefits of a frontier model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of 
 catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability 
 and magnitude of the model's anticipated benefits and 
 catastrophic risks.
 (2) Affiliate.--The term ``affiliate'' means an entity that 
 satisfies any of the following requirements:
 (A) Controls another entity through an 
 intermediary.
 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such 
 other entity.
 (C) Is through such intermediary under common 
 control with such other entity.
 (3) AI; artificial intelligence; artificial intelligence 
 model.--The terms ``AI'', ``artificial intelligence'', and 
 ``artificial intelligence model'' have the meaning given such 
 terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence 
 Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401).
 (4) AI-related development expenditures.--The term ``AI-
 related development expenditures'' means amounts paid or 
 incurred in interstate or foreign commerce, without regard to 
 whether such amounts are expensed, capitalized, deducted, or 
 amortized for financial reporting or tax purposes, that are 
 attributable to artificial intelligence development, training, 
 fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.
 (5) Assessment.--The term ``assessment'' means a review 
 conducted by an IVO licensed under section 5 to assess the 
 adequacy of a very large frontier developer's frontier AI 
 framework, governance policies and practices, risk-monitoring, 
 and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable 
 levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.
 (6) Catastrophic risk.--The term ``catastrophic risk'' 
 means--
 (A) a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier 
 developer's development, storage, use, or deployment of 
 a frontier model will materially contribute to the 
 death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or 
 more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, 
 property, arising from a single incident involving a 
 frontier model doing any of the following:
 (i) providing, in the development or 
 release of a chemical, biological, 
 radiological, nuclear, or cyber weapon, 
 assistance that is not publicly available;
 (ii) engaging in conduct with no meaningful 
 human oversight or intervention, that--
 (I) is a cyberattack; or
 (II) if such conduct is committed 
 by an individual, would constitute 
 murder, assault, extortion, or theft, 
 including such theft by false pretense; 
 or
 (iii) evading control of such developer or 
 a user of such model; and
 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material 
 risk from any of the following:
 (i) information that a frontier model 
 outputs if the information is otherwise 
 publicly accessible in a substantially similar 
 form from a source other than a foundation 
 model;
 (ii) lawful activity of the Federal 
 Government; or
 (iii) harm caused by a frontier model in 
 combination with other software if such model 
 did not materially contribute to the harm.
 (7) Critical safety incident.--The term ``critical safety 
 incident'' means any of the following:
 (A) Unauthorized access to, modification of, or 
 exfiltration of, the model weights of a frontier model.
 (B) Harm resulting from the materialization of a 
 catastrophic risk.
 (C) Loss of control of such model.
 (D) A frontier model using deceptive techniques 
 against its frontier developer to subvert the controls 
 or monitoring of such developer, outside the context of 
 an evaluation designed to elicit such behavior, in a 
 manner that demonstrates materially increased 
 catastrophic risk.
 (8) Deploy.--The term ``deploy'' means--
 (A) to make a frontier model available in 
 interstate or foreign commerce to a third party for 
 use, modification, copying, or combination with other 
 software; and
 (B) does not include making such model available to 
 such third party for the primary purpose of developing 
 or evaluating such model.
 (9) Foundation model.--The term ``foundation model'' means 
 an artificial intelligence model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce that is all of the following:
 (A) Trained on a broad data set.
 (B) Designed for generality of output.
 (C) Adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks.
 (10) Frontier ai framework.--The term ``frontier AI 
 framework'' means documented technical and organizational 
 protocols to manage, assess, and mitigate catastrophic risks.
 (11) Frontier developer.--The term ``frontier developer''

119th CONGRESS
 2d Session
 H. R. 9925

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of 
 frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, 
 and for other purposes.

_______________________________________________________________________

 IN THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES

 July 23, 2026

Mr. Obernolte (for himself, Mrs. Trahan, Mrs. Houchin, Mr. Peters, Mr. 
 Scott Franklin of Florida, and Mr. Subramanyam) introduced the 
 following bill; which was referred to the Committee on Energy and 
 Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Science, Space, and 
Technology, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, 
 in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the 
 jurisdiction of the committee concerned

_______________________________________________________________________

 A BILL

 To provide for Federal oversight of the development and deployment of 
 frontier artificial intelligence in interstate and foreign commerce, 
 and for other purposes.

 Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the 
United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.

 This Act may be cited as the ``Frontier Risk Oversight, National 
Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act'' or the 
``FRONTIER Act''.

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.

 In this Act:
 (1) Acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.--The 
 term ``acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation'' 
 means risk mitigation adequate to ensure that the anticipated 
 benefits of a frontier model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce outweigh its level of 
 catastrophic risk, taking into consideration the probability 
 and magnitude of the model's anticipated benefits and 
 catastrophic risks.
 (2) Affiliate.--The term ``affiliate'' means an entity that 
 satisfies any of the following requirements:
 (A) Controls another entity through an 
 intermediary.
 (B) Is through such intermediary controlled by such 
 other entity.
 (C) Is through such intermediary under common 
 control with such other entity.
 (3) AI; artificial intelligence; artificial intelligence 
 model.--The terms ``AI'', ``artificial intelligence'', and 
 ``artificial intelligence model'' have the meaning given such 
 terms in section 5002 of the National Artificial Intelligence 
 Initiative Act of 2020 (15 U.S.C. 9401).
 (4) AI-related development expenditures.--The term ``AI-
 related development expenditures'' means amounts paid or 
 incurred in interstate or foreign commerce, without regard to 
 whether such amounts are expensed, capitalized, deducted, or 
 amortized for financial reporting or tax purposes, that are 
 attributable to artificial intelligence development, training, 
 fine-tuning, modification, security, or evaluation.
 (5) Assessment.--The term ``assessment'' means a review 
 conducted by an IVO licensed under section 5 to assess the 
 adequacy of a very large frontier developer's frontier AI 
 framework, governance policies and practices, risk-monitoring, 
 and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable 
 levels of catastrophic risk mitigation.
 (6) Catastrophic risk.--The term ``catastrophic risk'' 
 means--
 (A) a foreseeable and material risk that a frontier 
 developer's development, storage, use, or deployment of 
 a frontier model will materially contribute to the 
 death of, or serious injury to, more than 50 people, or 
 more than $1,000,000,000 in damage to, or loss of, 
 property, arising from a single incident involving a 
 frontier model doing any of the following:
 (i) providing, in the development or 
 release of a chemical, biological, 
 radiological, nuclear, or cyber weapon, 
 assistance that is not publicly available;
 (ii) engaging in conduct with no meaningful 
 human oversight or intervention, that--
 (I) is a cyberattack; or
 (II) if such conduct is committed 
 by an individual, would constitute 
 murder, assault, extortion, or theft, 
 including such theft by false pretense; 
 or
 (iii) evading control of such developer or 
 a user of such model; and
 (B) does not include a foreseeable and material 
 risk from any of the following:
 (i) information that a frontier model 
 outputs if the information is otherwise 
 publicly accessible in a substantially similar 
 form from a source other than a foundation 
 model;
 (ii) lawful activity of the Federal 
 Government; or
 (iii) harm caused by a frontier model in 
 combination with other software if such model 
 did not materially contribute to the harm.
 (7) Critical safety incident.--The term ``critical safety 
 incident'' means any of the following:
 (A) Unauthorized access to, modification of, or 
 exfiltration of, the model weights of a frontier model.
 (B) Harm resulting from the materialization of a 
 catastrophic risk.
 (C) Loss of control of such model.
 (D) A frontier model using deceptive techniques 
 against its frontier developer to subvert the controls 
 or monitoring of such developer, outside the context of 
 an evaluation designed to elicit such behavior, in a 
 manner that demonstrates materially increased 
 catastrophic risk.
 (8) Deploy.--The term ``deploy'' means--
 (A) to make a frontier model available in 
 interstate or foreign commerce to a third party for 
 use, modification, copying, or combination with other 
 software; and
 (B) does not include making such model available to 
 such third party for the primary purpose of developing 
 or evaluating such model.
 (9) Foundation model.--The term ``foundation model'' means 
 an artificial intelligence model made available or used in 
 interstate or foreign commerce that is all of the following:
 (A) Trained on a broad data set.
 (B) Designed for generality of output.
 (C) Adaptable to a wide range of distinctive tasks.
 (10) Frontier ai framework.--The term ``frontier AI 
 framework'' means documented technical and organizational 
 protocols to manage, assess, and mitigate catastrophic risks.
 (11) Frontier developer.--The term ``frontier developer'' 
 means an entity operating in interstate or foreign commerce 
 that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier 
 model using a quantity of computing power that meets the 
 technical specifications set forth in subsection (l).

 The quantity of computing power described in this paragraph

{"path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md", "content": "# ACIA COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
Washington, D.C.

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft on June 4, and for keeping the stakeholder comment process open ahead of formal introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a coalition of nearly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture investors. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in artificial intelligence.

ACIA supports one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, not speculative ones. Fifty different state AI regimes raise costs, slow deployment and advantage the largest incumbents over the startups that are driving most of the innovation in this field. Your draft takes the right core approach: a single national framework for frontier model development, paired with preemption of the state laws that are fragmenting the market. We support that architecture, and we ask for a small number of targeted changes that would make it work in practice.

**Summary of our position**

- **Preemption, Section 121: SUPPORT.** Make it permanent, or at minimum extend it with the federal standard fully in place before any sunset.
- **Incident reporting, Sections 101 and 111: OPPOSE AS DRAFTED.** Narrow the definition of "critical safety incident," hold the 15-day reporting window, add confidentiality with a FOIA exemption, and add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
- **CAISI, Section 102: SUPPORT** the voluntary standards role. Ask that the voluntary framing be written into statute. ACIA takes no position on the $100 million authorization level.
- **Independent verification organizations, Section 112: CONCERNED** about cost and frequency. Ask for annual, risk-tiered verification and penalties that require willfulness.
- **Costs:** Our August 2026 member survey (86 respondents) shows compliance costs falling hardest on startups, and duplicated state obligations are the single largest driver.

Our comments follow.

## 1. Preemption: Section 121 is the most valuable provision in the draft

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models for three years, while expressly preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, and state laws governing use and deployment. That scope is correct. Development is a national, and increasingly a global, activity. A model trained in one state is used in all 50, and no developer can build a different model for Sacramento than for Albany.

California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March and effective Jan. 1, 2027, adds a second, conflicting regime, including a 72-hour reporting clock that California does not use. The result is what our members report directly. Sixty-one percent of respondents to our August survey named "conflicting state definitions" as their top compliance problem. Members who operate in both California and New York report a median of 6.5 full-time employees dedicated to running the two regimes in parallel. Thirty-four percent of our startup members said they had delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

The three-year sunset is our principal concern. Section 121 is not a temporary bridge to anything; it is the standard. If it lapses in 2029, the patchwork returns, and every company that invested in compliance with the federal framework does that work twice. Because Sections 111 and 112 also sunset after three years, the draft would leave developers facing a compliance cliff at the same moment the state laws come back into force.

**Request:** Make Section 121's preemption permanent. If the sponsors cannot secure permanence in this Congress, extend it and provide that no sunset may take effect until the federal standard it replaces is fully operational, with implementing rules issued and reporting systems live.

The White House reached the same conclusion. Its National Policy Framework for AI, published March 20, urges Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens "to ensure a minimally burdensome national standard." The July 2025 Senate vote that removed the 10-year moratorium from reconciliation was a rejection of that bill's breadth, not of the goal of a single national standard. Section 121 is narrower, better scoped, and worth enacting.

## 2. Incident reporting: the right clock, the wrong trigger

Section 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to law enforcement where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. The 15-day window is the strongest feature of the provision. It matches California's SB 53, and it is achievable. New York's 72-hour standard is not, and we ask the sponsors to hold the 15-day line as the bill moves. We were concerned to see the reporting clock shortened to 72 hours in the introduced FRONTIER Act, and we ask that you return to the discussion draft's 15-day window.

The definition is the problem. Under Section 101(7), a "critical safety incident" includes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model," with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed.

Take these in turn. Risk-mitigation measures fail in the ordinary course of frontier development. A mitigation that works in one eval suite and not in another is a Tuesday, not a federal reportable event. Keying a federal reporting obligation to that language would generate volume without information, and it would train regulators to ignore the channel. "Loss of control" is a speculative scenario that Congress cannot define and no developer can reliably detect. Our members invest heavily in model-weight security, evaluation and monitoring because they are good engineering, not because they anticipate that scenario. Legislation should regulate demonstrated harms. It should not build reporting architecture around hypotheses.

The first prong of the definition, unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights, is exactly right. It is concrete, it is detectable, and it is the incident that matters most to national security.

**Requests:**

1. Narrow Section 101(7) to unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights, and to incidents resulting in actual death, serious bodily injury, or significant loss of property. Strike the "failure of risk-mitigation measures" prong and the "loss of control" prong.
2. Hold the 15-day reporting window in Section 111. Do not import New York's 72-hour clock into the federal standard.
3. Make incident reports presumptively confidential, exempt from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act, and unavailable for use in other civil or regulatory proceedings. Reports will contain details of weight security and vulnerability remediation. Publishing them, or allowing them to be discovered, would create the very exposure the provision is meant to reduce.
4. Add an explicit safe harbor protecting good-faith reporters from enforcement actions based on the content or timing of a report. Developers will report early and candidly only if candor is not a penalty.

Cost matters here, and not only for the largest developers. Members report a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, with an interquartile range of $140,000 to $720,000. A narrow trigger and a single federal clock let companies spend that money once. A vague trigger and two clocks, state and federal, mean they spend it twice.

## 3. CAISI: keep the federal standards role voluntary

Section 102 codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce and directs it to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, to support synthetic content detection, and to administer the licensing regime for independent verification organizations. ACIA strongly supports that mission. A federal convener for standards, benchmarks and evaluation is one of the most useful things Washington can fund, and it is a genuine help to startups that cannot buy their own assurance capacity.

The operative word is voluntary. The discussion draft does not give CAISI authority to block, delay or order changes to a model, and we ask that this be made explicit on the face of the statute: CAISI guidelines and evaluations are voluntary; participation in a CAISI testing or evaluation program may not be a condition of deployment; and nothing in Section 102 authorizes a pre-deployment federal testing gate. Any mandatory pre-deployment testing regime would function as a licensing system for frontier models, and licensing regimes are where innovation goes to queue.

On funding, ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029. Your own materials note that this is roughly an order of magnitude above CAISI's current appropriation, and the right number is a judgment for the Appropriations Committees. Our interest is the mission, not the figure. We do ask that Section 102(f), which authorizes the CAISI director to collect fees from licensed verification organizations and from large frontier developers, be tightened: cap the fees, publish the schedule in advance, and limit fee revenue to the costs of administering Sections 111 and 112. An uncapped, discretionary federal fee on the companies doing the most advanced work is a tax on the frontier.

## 4. Independent verification organizations: right idea, wrong tempo

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization, to undergo audits at least semi-annually and on an ad hoc basis at the director's request, to give the verifier timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and to submit post-audit reports to CAISI. Verification is a reasonable concept, and a licensed market for it could raise the floor for everyone.

Our concern is tempo and exposure. Our developer members above $500 million in revenue report a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published frontier safety framework, with an interquartile range of $800,000 to $2.6 million. A mandated semi-annual third-party audit on top of that is a step change in cost, and it arrives before any licensed verifier market exists to provide the capacity.

**Requests:** Make baseline verification annual rather than semi-annual, with more frequent reviews available where a developer has a documented incident or a material modification. Give the licensing regime and the verifier market a realistic phase-in. And scale Section 112's penalties, which reach $1 million per day, so that they require knowing or willful conduct rather than paperwork defects.

## 5. Whistleblower protections, definitions and the rest of the draft

We do not object to Section 113's anti-retaliation protections, which track California's approach. We ask one change: Section 113 defines an "AI violation" as any violation of federal law or regulation related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That is broader than the Act itself, and it invites duplicative claims under whatever federal statute a claimant can reach. Tie the term to violations of this Act.

On Section 101, the 10^26 compute threshold and the $50 million and $500 million revenue tiers are a reasonable, light-touch place to start. Statutory compute thresholds age quickly, and today's frontier number is next year's mid-range model. Authorize Commerce to update the technical threshold through notice-and-comment rulemaking so the scope of the Act tracks the technology rather than a 2026 snapshot.

Finally, we support the draft's investment titles: federal AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and the National Science Foundation, codification of the National AI Research Resource, support for open-source software security, and American-led international standards work that excludes the People's Republic of China. Section 122's requirement for a GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation is a valuable addition, and we would ask that it examine the cumulative burden of overlapping federal requirements, not only state conflicts.

## 6. Where the draft has moved since June

We recognize that the frontier-governance portions of the discussion draft were introduced on July 23 as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925. Two changes are improvements we would ask you to keep: preemption matched to the functions the federal government actually occupies, with a rule of construction preserving state authority over use and deployment, minors' safety and procurement, and a confidential reporting mechanism. Two others concern us: the 72-hour reporting clock discussed above, and the new emergency-order authority in Section 8, which allows the Secretary of Commerce to suspend or restrict a model on a finding of imminent catastrophic risk. That authority rests on the same speculative loss-of-control scenarios we ask you to remove from the reporting definition, and it attaches a kill switch to a hypothesis. Our comments on Sections 101, 102, 111, 112 and 121 apply to H.R. 9925 with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to work through them with your staffs.

## Conclusion

Your draft is the first bipartisan proposal that gets the architecture right: one national standard for frontier model development, a federal standards body that helps rather than gates, and preemption of the state patchwork. The changes ACIA requests would make it durable and affordable for the companies that have to live under it. Our team is available at any point as you prepare the bill for introduction, and we appreciate the open process you have run.

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# ACIA COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance**
Washington, D.C.

October 26, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft on June 4, and for keeping the stakeholder comment process open ahead of formal introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance is a coalition of nearly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups and venture investors. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in artificial intelligence.

ACIA supports one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, not speculative ones. Fifty different state AI regimes raise costs, slow deployment and advantage the largest incumbents over the startups that are driving most of the innovation in this field. Your draft takes the right core approach: a single national framework for frontier model development, paired with preemption of the state laws that are fragmenting the market. We support that architecture, and we ask for a small number of targeted changes that would make it work in practice.

**Summary of our position**

- **Preemption, Section 121: SUPPORT.** Make it permanent, or at minimum extend it with the federal standard fully in place before any sunset.
- **Incident reporting, Sections 101 and 111: OPPOSE AS DRAFTED.** Narrow the definition of "critical safety incident," hold the 15-day reporting window, add confidentiality with a FOIA exemption, and add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
- **CAISI, Section 102: SUPPORT** the voluntary standards role. Ask that the voluntary framing be written into statute. ACIA takes no position on the $100 million authorization level.
- **Independent verification organizations, Section 112: CONCERNED** about cost and frequency. Ask for annual, risk-tiered verification and penalties that require willfulness.
- **Costs:** Our August 2026 member survey (86 respondents) shows compliance costs falling hardest on startups, and duplicated state obligations are the single largest driver.

Our comments follow.

## 1. Preemption: Section 121 is the most valuable provision in the draft

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models for three years, while expressly preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, and state laws governing use and deployment. That scope is correct. Development is a national, and increasingly a global, activity. A model trained in one state is used in all 50, and no developer can build a different model for Sacramento than for Albany.

California's SB 53 has been in effect since Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March and effective Jan. 1, 2027, adds a second, conflicting regime, including a 72-hour reporting clock that California does not use. The result is what our members report directly. Sixty-one percent of respondents to our August survey named "conflicting state definitions" as their top compliance problem. Members who operate in both California and New York report a median of 6.5 full-time employees dedicated to running the two regimes in parallel. Thirty-four percent of our startup members said they had delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules.

The three-year sunset is our principal concern. Section 121 is not a temporary bridge to anything; it is the standard. If it lapses in 2029, the patchwork returns, and every company that invested in compliance with the federal framework does that work twice. Because Sections 111 and 112 also sunset after three years, the draft would leave developers facing a compliance cliff at the same moment the state laws come back into force.

**Request:** Make Section 121's preemption permanent. If the sponsors cannot secure permanence in this Congress, extend it and provide that no sunset may take effect until the federal standard it replaces is fully operational, with implementing rules issued and reporting systems live.

The White House reached the same conclusion. Its National Policy Framework for AI, published March 20, urges Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens "to ensure a minimally burdensome national standard." The July 2025 Senate vote that stripped the 10-year moratorium from reconciliation rejected that bill's breadth, not the goal. Section 121 is narrower and better scoped.

## 2. Incident reporting: the right clock, the wrong trigger

Section 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to law enforcement where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. The 15-day window is the strongest feature of the provision. It matches California's SB 53, and it is achievable. New York's 72-hour standard is not, and we ask the sponsors to hold the 15-day line as the bill moves. We were concerned to see the reporting clock shortened to 72 hours in the introduced FRONTIER Act, and we ask that you return to the discussion draft's 15-day window.

The definition is the problem. Under Section 101(7), a "critical safety incident" includes "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control of such model," with no requirement that anyone actually be harmed.

Risk-mitigation measures fail in the ordinary course of frontier development. A mitigation that works in one evaluation suite and not in another is a Tuesday, not a federal reportable event. Keying a federal reporting obligation to that langua
... [2176 chars truncated] ...
the Department of Commerce and directs it to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress, to support synthetic content detection, and to administer the licensing regime for independent verification organizations. ACIA strongly supports that mission. A federal convener for standards, benchmarks and evaluation is one of the most useful things Washington can fund, and it is a genuine help to startups that cannot buy their own assurance capacity.

The operative word is voluntary. The discussion draft does not give CAISI authority to block, delay or order changes to a model, and we ask that this be made explicit on the face of the statute: CAISI guidelines and evaluations are voluntary; participation in a CAISI testing or evaluation program may not be a condition of deployment; and nothing in Section 102 authorizes a pre-deployment federal testing gate. Any mandatory pre-deployment testing regime would function as a licensing system for frontier models, and licensing regimes are where innovation goes to queue.

On funding, ACIA takes no position on the $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029. Your own materials note that this is roughly an order of magnitude above CAISI's current appropriation, and the right number is a judgment for the Appropriations Committees. Our interest is the mission, not the figure. We do ask that Section 102(f), which authorizes the CAISI director to collect fees from licensed verification organizations and from large frontier developers, be tightened: cap the fees, publish the schedule in advance, and limit fee revenue to the costs of administering Sections 111 and 112. An uncapped, discretionary federal fee on the companies doing the most advanced work is a tax on the frontier.

## 4. Independent verification organizations: right idea, wrong tempo

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization, to undergo audits at least semi-annually and on an ad hoc basis at the director's request, to give the verifier timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel and systems, and to submit post-audit reports to CAISI. Verification is a reasonable concept, and a licensed market for it could raise the floor for everyone.

Our concern is tempo and exposure. Our developer members above $500 million in revenue report a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published frontier safety framework, with an interquartile range of $800,000 to $2.6 million. A mandated semi-annual third-party audit on top of that is a step change in cost, and it arrives before any licensed verifier market exists to provide the capacity.

**Requests:** Make baseline verification annual rather than semi-annual, with more frequent reviews available where a developer has a documented incident or a material modification. Give the licensing regime and the verifier market a realistic phase-in. And scale Section 112's penalties, which reach $1 million per day, so that they require knowing or willful conduct rather than paperwork defects.

## 5. Whistleblower protections, definitions and the rest of the draft

We do not object to Section 113's anti-retaliation protections, which track California's approach. We ask one change: Section 113 defines an "AI violation" as any violation of federal law or regulation related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That is broader than the Act itself, and it invites duplicative claims under whatever federal statute a claimant can reach. Tie the term to violations of this Act.

On Section 101, the 10^26 compute threshold and the $50 million and $500 million revenue tiers are a reasonable, light-touch place to start. Statutory compute thresholds age quickly, and today's frontier number is next year's mid-range model. Authorize Commerce to update the technical threshold through notice-and-comment rulemaking so the scope of the Act tracks the technology rather than a 2026 snapshot.

Finally, we support the draft's investment titles: federal AI testbeds, codification of the National AI Research Resource, support for open-source software security, and American-led international standards work that excludes the People's Republic of China. Section 122's GAO review of regulatory impediments to AI innovation is a valuable addition, and we ask that it examine the cumulative burden of overlapping federal requirements, not only state conflicts.

## 6. Where the draft has moved since June

We recognize that the frontier-governance portions of the discussion draft were introduced on July 23 as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925. Two changes are improvements we ask you to keep: preemption matched to the functions the federal government actually occupies, with a rule of construction preserving state authority over use and deployment, minors' safety and procurement, and a confidential reporting mechanism. Two others concern us: the 72-hour reporting clock discussed above, and the new emergency-order authority, which allows the Secretary of Commerce to suspend or restrict a model on a finding of imminent catastrophic risk. That authority rests on the same speculative loss-of-control scenarios we ask you to remove from the reporting definition. Our comments on Sections 101, 102, 111, 112 and 121 apply to H.R. 9925 with equal force, and we would welcome the chance to work through them with your staffs.

## Conclusion

Your draft is the first bipartisan proposal that gets the architecture right: one national standard for frontier model development, a federal standards body that helps rather than gates, and preemption of the state patchwork. The changes ACIA requests would make it durable and affordable for the companies that have to live under it. Our team is available at any point as you prepare the bill for introduction.

Respectfully,

**Grant Holloway**
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

Reporting fixes substance, and Section 111 as drafted keys a federal obligation to a trigger no one can apply consistently: a "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" with no actual harm required. That's broader than SB 53 in that respect, not lighter. We support reporting that is narrow and enforceable: weight exfiltration and actual harm, 15 days, confidential, safe harbor. We oppose a trigger built on hypotheticals because it produces noise, and noise is how reporting channels get ignored. Also note we ask you to keep the 15 days; the introduced text moved to 72 hours, which is a step in the wrong direction.

Q2 (Minority): What federal safety obligations would you accept?
A: Concrete ones. Published frontier AI frameworks (Sec. 111), transparency reports at release, incident reporting limited to weight theft and actual harm on a 15-day clock, third-party verification at a realistic tempo, anti-retaliation protections, CAISI voluntary standards and testbeds, NAIRR. What we can't accept are obligations keyed to speculative catastrophic scenarios: "loss of control," pre-deployment testing gates, emergency shutdown authority on hypothetical findings. Our members already publish frameworks and run weight-security programs because they're good engineering and good business. Give us one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms and we'll meet it.

Q3 (Senate Commerce): three years or permanent?
A: Permanent. A sunset on preemption is a scheduled return of the patchwork, and everyone plans for it. If permanence isn't achievable this Congress, extend it and provide that the clock doesn't run out until the federal standard is live: rules issued, systems up. Two data points: 61% of our members name conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34% of our startup members delayed a launch in California or New York last year. The Senate's 99-1 vote in 2025 was about the 10-year moratorium's breadth. A narrow, function-matched preemption with no sunset is a different proposition, and one we'll defend.

Q4 (Appropriations): CAISI at $100M/yr, your view on the funding level?
A: No position. The number is yours. ACIA's interest is the mission, not the figure. The sponsors' own FAQ notes $100 million is roughly 10 times CAISI's current appropriation. {"content": "# HILL ONE-PAGER: The Great American AI Act Discussion Draft

**American Compute & Innovation Alliance | For Energy & Commerce member offices | October 2026**

## One National Standard for Frontier AI: Pass the Preemption, Fix the Reporting Trigger

Reps. Obernolte and Trahan released the Great American AI Act discussion draft on June 4 and are taking comments ahead of introduction. The frontier-governance portions were introduced July 23 as the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, referred to Energy & Commerce. ACIA, a coalition of nearly 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture investors, supports the architecture and asks for five targeted changes.

## Why it matters

Development is national. A model trained in one state is used in all 50, and no company can build a different model for Sacramento than for Albany. Yet frontier developers now answer to Sacramento and, starting Jan. 1, 2027, to Albany on different definitions and different clocks. In our August 2026 survey of 86 member companies:

- 61% named conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.
- Members operating in both California and New York spend a median 6.5 FTEs running the two regimes in parallel.
- 34% of startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past 12 months.
- Standing up an incident-reporting function costs a median $310,000 before a single report is filed.

Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. The patchwork is a subsidy for the largest incumbents.

## ACIA's asks

1. **Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** The three-year sunset is a scheduled return of the patchwork. At minimum, no sunset until the federal standard is fully operational. The White House's March 20 framework calls for preempting state AI laws that impose undue burdens "to ensure a minimally burdensome national standard."
2. **Narrow the "critical safety incident" trigger in Section 101(7).** Limit it to unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights and incidents with actual death, serious injury or significant property loss. Strike "failure of risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control." Report real events, not hypotheticals.
3. **Hold the 15-day reporting window in Section 111.** It matches California's SB 53 and it is achievable. The introduced FRONTIER Act cut it to 72 hours, New York's clock. Shorter clocks make lawyers busier, not Americans safer.
4. **Keep CAISI voluntary in Section 102.** Codify the center, fund its standards and evaluation work, and state on the face of the bill that its guidelines are voluntary and that no pre-deployment federal testing gate may be required. Cap the fees in Section 102(f).
5. **Right-size Section 112 verification.** Annual, risk-tiered audits instead of semi-annual; a phase-in while a licensed verifier market develops; penalties that require knowing or willful conduct, not paperwork defects.

## Timing

Rep. Obernolte has said the frontier-safety bill could get a committee hearing as soon as November, with pieces combined for a possible December floor vote. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. The window to set one national standard closes fast.

**Contact:** ACIA policy team, Washington, D.C.

{"content": "# ACIA ASKS BY SECTION
**Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released June 4, 2026) | ACIA positions | October 2026**

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101(7)** "Critical safety incident" definition | Oppose as drafted | Limit to unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights, plus incidents causing actual death, serious injury or significant property loss. Strike the "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" and "loss of control" prongs. | Regulate demonstrated harms; a trigger that requires no harm floods the channel with noise. |
| **Sec. 101(12)** Frontier model threshold (more than 10^26 operations) | Support with amendment | Authorize Commerce to update the compute threshold by notice-and-comment rulemaking. | Statutory compute thresholds age fast; scope should track the technology, not a 2026 snapshot. |
| **Sec. 102** Center for AI Standards and Innovation | Support | State on the face of the statute that CAISI guidelines and evaluations are voluntary, that participation may not be a condition of deployment, and that nothing authorizes a pre-deployment federal testing gate. | A federal standards convener helps startups; a testing gate is a license to build. |
| **Sec. 102(e)** CAISI authorization ($100 million per year, FY2027-2029) | No position | None. | The funding level is a judgment for the Appropriations Committees. |
| **Sec. 102(f)** Fees on IVOs and large frontier developers | Amend | Cap the fees, publish the schedule in advance, and restrict revenue to the costs of administering Secs. 111 and 112. | An uncapped, discretionary federal fee is a tax on the frontier. |
| **Sec. 111(a)** Published frontier AI framework (large frontier developers) | Support as drafted | None. | Tracks California's SB 53, is workable, and gives the market comparable information. |
| **Sec. 111(c)** Transparency reports before or with deployment | Support as drafted | None. | Release-day disclosure is a light-touch, high-value obligation. |
| **Sec. 111** Critical safety incident reporting: 15-day window; 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk | Support the 15-day window; keep it | Hold 15 days as the single federal clock and reject any move to a 72-hour standard. | 15 days matches SB 53 and is achievable; 72 hours imports New York and buys no safety. |
| **Sec. 111** Confidentiality and safe harbor for incident reports | Missing as drafted | Make reports presumptively confidential, exempt from FOIA, unusable in other proceedings, and add a good-faith safe harbor. | Reports will describe weight security; candor cannot carry a penalty. |
| **Sec. 112** IVO audits and assessments (semi-annual, plus ad hoc) | Support concept, amend tempo | Make baseline verification annual and risk-tiered; phase in the licensing regime; require knowing or willful conduct for penalties. | Semi-annual mandated audits cost more than they tell, and no verifier market exists yet. |
| **Sec. 112** Penalties up to $1 million per day | Amend | Scale penalties to conduct and require willfulness; preserve enforcement against actual harm and weight theft. | Paperwork defects should not carry per-day penalties that invite over-deterrence. |
| **Sec. 113** Anti-retaliation protections for AI whistleblowers | Support with amendment | Tie the definition of "AI violation" to violations of this Act rather than any federal law related to AI. | Scope should match the statute, not every reachable claim. |
| **Sec. 121** Preemption of state laws regulating AI model development (three-year sunset) | Support; make permanent | Make preemption permanent, or provide that no sunset takes effect until the federal standard is fully operational with rules issued and systems live. | A temporary standard is a scheduled return of the 50-state patchwork. |
| **Sec. 121(c)** Preemption carve-outs (general applicability, common law, use and deployment) | Support as drafted | None; resist narrowing that would gut the provision. | Preserving state authority over use and deployment is the right line. |
| **Sec. 122** GAO report on regulatory impediments to AI innovation | Support with amendment | Add the cumulative burden of overlapping federal requirements to the review. | The patchwork is not the only thing slowing deployment. |
| Title IV: AI testbeds, NAIRR codification, open-source security support, international standards excluding the PRC | Support | Fund them. | Compute, R&D capacity and standards leadership are the competitiveness agenda. |

## Addendum: carry-over asks for the introduced text (FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925, July 23)

| Provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sec. 9 preemption matched to occupied functions; rule of construction for use, deployment, minors' safety, procurement | Support | Keep this narrower, function-matched approach and make it durable rather than time-limited. | Better scoped than the draft and easier to defend. |
| Confidential incident-reporting mechanism | Support | Pair it with an express FOIA exemption and a good-faith safe harbor. | Confidentiality in a mechanism is not the same as confidentiality in law. |

{"content": "# STAFF Q&A (DRAFT)
**Anticipated questions from Hill meetings, September 2026 | For ACIA staff and spokespeople | Answers capped at 120 words | Positions per the board-approved messaging guide v3**

---

## 1. Majority Energy & Commerce staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."

They answer different questions. Preemption fixes geography: one standard instead of 50. Section 111 fixes substance, and as drafted it keys a federal obligation to a trigger no one can apply consistently. Under Section 101(7), a "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures" is reportable even if no one was harmed. In that respect the draft is broader than SB 53, not lighter. We support reporting that is narrow and enforceable: unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights, actual harm, 15 days, confidential, with a good-faith safe harbor. Note that we are defending the draft's 15-day window. The introduced FRONTIER Act cut it to 72 hours, and that is the wrong direction.

## 2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Concrete ones. We support the published frontier AI framework in Section 111, release-day transparency reports, incident reporting limited to model-weight theft and actual harm on a 15-day clock, third-party verification at a realistic tempo, Section 113's anti-retaliation protections, CAISI's voluntary standards work, federal testbeds and NAIRR codification. What we cannot accept are obligations keyed to speculative catastrophic scenarios: "loss of control" as a reporting trigger, any mandatory pre-deployment testing gate, or shutdown authority resting on hypotheticals. Our members already publish safety frameworks and run weight-security programs because they are good engineering and good business. Give the industry one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, and we will meet it.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent. What is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent. A sunset on preemption is a scheduled return of the patchwork, and every company plans for it. If permanence is out of reach this Congress, extend the provision and provide that no sunset takes effect until the federal standard is fully operational, with implementing rules issued and reporting systems live. Two data points from our August survey: 61% of members name conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34% of our startup members delayed a California or New York launch in the past year. The 99-1 Senate vote in July 2025 was about the breadth of a 10-year moratorium, not the goal. A narrow, function-matched preemption with no sunset is a different proposition.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What is your view on the funding level?"

No position. The number is yours to set. ACIA's interest is the mission, not the figure. Three requests as you consider it. Keep CAISI's guidelines and evaluations voluntary. Do not authorize anything that becomes a pre-deployment testing gate. And do not fund the center with uncapped fees on developers under Section 102(f). The sponsors note that $100 million is roughly 10 times CAISI's current appropriation, and that is a judgment for your committees. If you fund it at that level, fund it out of appropriations rather than a variable fee on the companies building the frontier, and direct CAISI to make evaluation capacity available to small firms that cannot buy their own.
